Intel (INTC) reports earnings tomorrow: what to expect

Computer processor maker Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) will be reporting earnings this Thursday after the bell. Here's what to look for.

Intel beat analysts' revenue expectations last quarter, reporting revenues of $16.13 billion, up 25.4% year on year. It was an incredible quarter for the company, with a significant improvement in its inventory levels and a beat of analysts' EPS estimates.

Is Intel a buy or sell going into earnings? Read our full analysis here, it's free for active Edge members.

This quarter, the market is expecting Intel's revenue to grow 20.3% year on year, improving from the 2.8% increase it recorded in the same quarter last year.

Intel total revenue

Analysts covering the company have generally reconfirmed their estimates over the last 30 days, suggesting they anticipate the business will stay the course heading into earnings. Intel has a history of exceeding Wall Street's expectations.

Looking at Intel's peers in the semiconductors segment, some have already reported their Q3 results, giving us a hint as to what we can expect. Penguin Solutions delivered year-on-year revenue growth of 67.7%, beating analysts' expectations by 8.8%, and Western Digital reported revenues up 55.5%, topping estimates by 5.2%. Penguin Solutions traded up 13.1% following the results while Western Digital was down 3.4%.

Read our full analysis of Penguin Solutions's results here and Western Digital's results here.

In the last year or so, investors have shifted their focus from one macro dynamic to the next (AI disintermediation and AI investment to geopolitical conflict, interest rates, and the health of the wider economy). While some of the semiconductors stocks have shown solid performance in this choppy environment, the group has generally underperformed, with share prices down 8.3% on average over the last month. Intel is down 18.9% during the same time and is heading into earnings with an average analyst price target of $117.71 (compared to the current share price of $94.12).

Much of the decline looks like a pullback after an enormous run. Even after the slide, Intel stock is up 154% year to date (YTD), and it traded at $123 on September 25. A quantum acquisition is the newest chapter in the Intel story. The company didn't disclose terms, but Bloomberg put the price at about $2.3 billion. Classiq's platform helps developers design quantum algorithms and run them on different types of quantum hardware, which pairs with Intel's years of work on silicon-based spin qubits.

title: Intel Just Made a $2.3 Billion Quantum Buy and Is Spending Again. Can Cash Flow Keep Up?

Intel Just Made a $2.3 Billion Quantum Buy and Is Spending Again. Can Cash Flow Keep Up?

Trade Intel on Coinbase

Intel Just Made a $2.3 Billion Quantum Buy and Is Spending Again. Can Cash Flow Keep Up? ©MangoStar_Studio from Getty Images and Изображения пользователя Axel Makhalov via Canva
Key Takeaways

Intel agreed to buy quantum software company Classiq in a deal reportedly worth $2.3 billion, three days before its third-quarter report on Thursday, Oct. 29.

Intel's August share sale raised more than $20 billion, which gives it room to fund this year's spending without going back to the debt or equity markets.

Capex ran above cash from operations every year from 2022 through 2025, and total debt rose from $38.2 billion at the end of 2021 to $47.1 billion at the end of 2025.

The number to watch is Intel's 2027 capex plan: analysts expect $26.0 billion of capex and negative free cash flow of $1.4 billion that year.

Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) agreed on Monday to buy quantum software company Classiq, in a deal Bloomberg reported is worth about $2.3 billion. Intel didn't give a price, but CEO Lip-Bu Tan said in its announcement: "Joining forces with Classiq transforms Intel's Quantum Computing Group into a full-stack quantum computing business."

That's the second sign in a week that Intel is spending again. Ian King said on last week's Bloomberg Tech podcast that Intel's latest factory updates were "Intel saying we're starting spending money again." In Ohio, King noted, Intel built the concrete slabs, stopped, and is now putting the roof on.

So when Intel reports third-quarter results on Thursday, Oct. 29, after the close, the big question is whether its own cash flow can pay for all of it.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Intel, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Intel's Analyst Ratings

The last build-out didn't pay for itself

Intel has been here before. Cash from operations fell from $29.5 billion in 2021 to $9.7 billion in 2025. Capex ran above it every year from 2022 on, and peaked at $25.8 billion in 2023.

Intel (INTC): cash from operations vs. capital expenditures, $ billions, fiscal 2021–2025 (TIKR)

That added up to $44.3 billion of negative free cash flow from 2022 through 2025.

Intel filled the hole with borrowing, government money and new stock. Total debt rose from $38.2 billion at the end of 2021 to $47.1 billion at the end of 2025. Cash jumped in 2025 after Intel sold stock to the U.S. government, SoftBank and NVIDIA, and Washington sped up $5.7 billion of CHIPS Act funding.

Intel (INTC): total debt vs. cash and short-term investments, $ billions, fiscal 2021–2025 (TIKR)

And by June 27, 2026, total debt was back up to $50.5 billion.

This time, the money's already in the bank

The difference now is that Intel raised the money before the spending restarted. It held $29.7 billion of cash and short-term investments on June 27. Then in August it raised more than $20 billion selling new shares at $95 apiece.

On October 22, 2026, the Commerce Department signed letters of intent for $389 million in CHIPS Act research awards to four private companies. As a condition of each award, the department takes "a minority, non-controlling, non-voting equity stake". Helion is in line for up to $175 million, Commonwealth Fusion Systems for $85 million, Vertical Semiconductor for $73 million, and Sibelco for $56 million.

24/7 Wall St.

Tad DeHaven, a policy analyst at the Cato Institute, says those deals bring the count of announced or completed stakes to 40. No agency releases an official list.

The Council on Foreign Relations counts 43 because it includes Development Finance Corporation deals. Fortune counted 30 in July. At the time, a Treasury spokesperson said agencies report equity "in different ways." When nobody keeps one official record, it is hard to know what this shareholder actually owns.

A letter of intent comes before a final agreement, so part of DeHaven's 40 is still unsigned. In July 2026, National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said the stakes were "like a down payment on a sovereign wealth fund, which many countries have."

The pushback against OKX and ICE's tokenized stock venue now includes the biggest bank in the U.S.

JPMorgan Chase, Coca-Cola, and Dell Technologies are among seven companies added to OKXICE TSV's list of objecting issuers in a notice dated Tuesday. Advanced Micro Devices, Adobe, Applied Materials, and Sandisk round out the group. The additions bring the total to 33, up from 26 a day earlier.

Myriad: Which company will IPO next? Click to make your prediction.

The list has grown quickly. It stood at nine on Oct. 15, 16 on Oct. 19, and 22 on Oct. 23. Earlier objectors include Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, Intel, and Oracle. JPMorgan is the third major bank to object, after Goldman and Wells Fargo.

Under the SEC's innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate, a venue must notify a company before offering a version of its shares tokenized by an unaffiliated third party. If the company objects in writing within 30 days, the venue can't make that stock available for trading, according to the SEC's order. The objection applies only to that venue. The notices haven't disclosed the companies' reasons.

OKXICE's original Oct. 4 notice proposed 63 tokenized stocks from 62 companies, and several objectors, including Wells Fargo and Arm, weren't on that initial roster. Some of the biggest names, including Nvidia, Tesla, Apple, and Amazon, haven't objected so far.

OKXICE TSV, a 50-50 joint venture between NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange and OKX's U.S. holding company, plans to let approved users trade tokenized U.S. stocks 24/7. Trades would run through permissioned Uniswap v4 pools on OKX's XLayer blockchain, paired with stablecoins such as USDC. Earlier notices warned that it's uncertain whether tokenized shares in self-custodied wallets would be covered by the Securities Investor Protection Corporation if the tokenizer's broker-dealer failed.

OKX and ICE first teamed up on tokenized securities earlier this year before announcing the 24/7 venue this month. Nasdaq, which won SEC approval for its own tokenized securities pilot, has said it will opt its shares out of the exemption.
